transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Well... I guess I'm here because of a bathroom mirror, which I know sounds completely ridiculous when I say it out loud. We recently decided to do some minor updates to our master bathroom—nothing major, just painting and swapping out the old fixtures—and we put in one of those new, really bright LED mirrors. I thought it would be great for getting ready in the mornings before I head into the law firm. I'm a paralegal, so I have to look professional and put-together for work. 

But honestly, ever since we put that brighter mirror in, I just... I keep noticing my face, and it's driving me crazy. Specifically, the skin right around my cheeks and my jawline. It just looks so uneven to me now, and kind of saggy? Like, I know I'm 46 and I'm not in my twenties anymore, but it just looks so obvious and terrible to me now. I'll go in there to brush my teeth and I just end up standing there, staring at my jaw, tilting my head all different ways, pulling the skin back a little bit to see how it's supposed to look. 

I've pointed it out to my husband so many times. I'll stand right under the light and show him exactly where the skin is drooping and looking textured, and he just looks at me and swears he can't really see what I'm talking about. He says I look exactly the same as I did before we bought the mirror and that I'm making a big deal out of nothing. But I can see it. It's right there, and it's just taking up so much of my mental energy lately because I just can't stop focusing on it.
How much is this concern about your facial skin affecting your ability to focus on your daily tasks or enjoy your usual activities?

Well, I mean, I still get my work done. I have to, right? The attorneys at the firm rely on me, and you can't exactly miss a filing deadline just because you're unhappy with your reflection. But... it is definitely having an impact, especially in the mornings. 

I just get so caught up in front of that mirror now. I'll try applying my makeup differently, or I'll try to contour my jawline to somehow hide the sagging or the unevenness, and I'll wipe it off and try again, and suddenly I realize I've been standing there for an extra thirty or forty minutes. Because of that extra time I'm spending, I've actually had to rush into the courthouse a few mornings. I'm literally speed-walking in my work heels just to make it on time, feeling completely frantic, which just starts the whole day off on this incredibly stressful note. 

And it's not just work, it's my personal time, too. I go to this lovely yoga studio a couple of times a week—it usually really helps me decompress from all the legal paperwork—but I've missed the start of class more than once lately. I end up walking in late and having to unroll my mat in the back while everyone else is already doing their centering breaths, all because I couldn't pull myself away from scrutinizing my cheeks before I left the house. 

And, oh, the photos... that's been another big thing. I'm in a local book club, and we go to a few community events together, and there's always someone pulling out a phone to take a group picture for Facebook or whatever. Lately, I've just been volunteering to be the one to take the picture, or I'll just quietly step out of the frame to go grab a drink. I've skipped being in quite a few casual photos lately because I know if I'm in them, I won't be able to pay attention to the book discussion or enjoy the event. I'll just sit there the whole time worrying about how my face is going to look when they post it, zooming in on my jaw in my head. 

So, I guess I'm still doing my usual things, mostly, but it's just constantly hovering there, making everything a little harder and more exhausting than it needs to be.
Have you noticed yourself becoming concerned about any other parts of your face or body, or is your main focus specifically on the skin around your cheeks and jawline?

No, it really is just the skin around my cheeks and jaw. I mean, obviously, I have other things that aren't perfect, right? Like, I've got a little bit of a stomach from having my two boys, and my hair isn't as thick as it used to be when I was in my twenties, but none of that bothers me. I mean, I don't love it, but I don't stand there staring at it. I don't obsess over it. I just put on a looser blouse or use a volumizing shampoo and go about my day. 

But this thing with my face... it's just so different. It's like I have tunnel vision for it. I'll look in the mirror, and it's literally the only thing I can see. I don't even look at my eyes or my nose or anything else. It's just straight to the jawline. It's so strange because I never used to be like this. I was always the kind of person who could get ready in fifteen minutes flat—shower, quick makeup, throw the hair up, out the door. My husband used to brag about how low-maintenance I was compared to some of his friends' wives. And now, I'm the one holding us up because I can't stop looking at this one specific area. 

I even bought this magnifying mirror to put on my vanity table, thinking maybe if I could just see it closer, I could figure out a way to fix it with concealer or something. But that just made it worse, obviously, because then I'm just looking at the exact same spot, just ten times bigger. So no, I really don't think I'm worried about anything else. It's just this one very specific, very frustrating thing that I can't seem to get out of my head.

When you're looking in the mirror and focusing on your jawline, do you feel driven to perform certain repetitive behaviors or mental acts—like checking, measuring, comparing, or trying to 'fix' it in your mind—to try to reduce your distress?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. I mean, it's become this whole ordeal. Most mornings, I end up checking my face from a few different angles, over and over. I'll stand there and turn my head to the left, then to the right, then I'll tilt my chin up, and then tuck it down, just trying to see exactly how the shadows are falling on my jaw and if the sagging looks worse from one side than the other. 

And because of that, I almost always end up putting on a little extra makeup before I leave for the courthouse. I actually went out and bought this special contouring powder, and I'll stand there trying to paint a shadow under my jaw to hide the unevenness. I'll blend it and blend it, and sometimes I think I've put on too much, so I have to take a tissue and wipe it off, which just makes my skin red, and then I have to start all over with my foundation. It's just this constant cycle of trying to fix it before I can even walk out the door. 

And then once I'm actually at work... yes, the comparing is constant. I'll be in the breakroom or walking files over to one of the partners, and I find myself comparing my face to the women I see at work. Especially the younger attorneys who are fresh out of law school, but honestly, even the other paralegals who are my age. I'll literally be standing there while they're talking to me about a deposition, and I'm not even looking at their eyes—I'm just staring at their jawlines, comparing them to mine, wondering how their skin still looks so firm and why mine looks so terrible. 

And I know I mentioned the photos earlier, but it really is a deliberate thing now. I will completely avoid being in casual pictures if I’m not feeling okay about it. If my makeup didn't go on right that morning, or if I feel like the lighting in the room is too harsh and overhead, I just can't do it. My sister wanted to take a quick selfie when we grabbed lunch the other day just to send to our mom, and I literally pretended I had to use the restroom right that second just to get out of it. I just couldn't bear the thought of my jawline looking saggy in the picture and then having to look at it later. It's just... it's exhausting, having to manage all these little things just to get through a normal day.
Has this concern about your jawline ever caused you to avoid social situations, or made you feel so upset that it was hard to function normally in your day-to-day life?

Well, like I was mentioning a little bit earlier, I haven't completely stopped functioning or anything drastic like that. I do still get my work done. I mean, as a paralegal, you really don't have the luxury of just dropping the ball because you're having a bad morning in front of the mirror. The attorneys need their briefs, the filings have strict deadlines, so I push through it. 

But, you know, the extra time I spend getting ready... it really does take a toll. Like I said about rushing into the courthouse—it just throws off my entire morning rhythm. I'll be speed-walking from the parking garage, my heart is pounding, I'm practically sweating in my work clothes, and it's all just because I was stuck in my bathroom for an extra thirty minutes trying to make my jawline look acceptable. It makes me feel so unprofessional when I arrive feeling that frantic. 

And it's the same with my yoga classes. I haven't stopped going, because I really do need that time to stretch and unwind, but missing the start of class more than once has been so incredibly frustrating. Walking into that studio when the room is completely silent and everyone is already on their mats doing their centering breaths... the instructor always gives you that little sympathetic but annoyed look, you know? It's humiliating. I'm paying for this class to relax, and instead, I'm starting it feeling embarrassed and stressed, all because I couldn't step away from the mirror.

As for social things, I still go to my book club and the different community events we attend. I love the women in that group. But, like I touched on before, the photos are where I really pull back and avoid things. I'll go to the event, but the second someone says, "Oh, let's get a group picture!" I just... I panic a little inside. I'll immediately volunteer to take it, or I'll pretend I need to grab an appetizer or check a text message. I've skipped being in so many casual photos with them lately, just entirely opted out, because I know if I don't, I will spend the rest of the evening completely distracted. I won't hear a word anyone is saying about the book we read because I'll just be agonizing over how my sagging skin is going to look when they inevitably post the picture online. So I guess I am still functioning and doing my day-to-day things, but it's just this constant, heavy weight making all of it so much harder and more stressful than it ever used to be.

Can you describe how you feel about your jawline when you look at it—do you feel like it looks abnormal or unattractive in a way that makes you feel defective or disfigured, or is it more about the appearance bothering you without feeling like it defines how you see yourself overall?

Defective... gosh, that’s a really heavy word, isn't it? I don't know if I would go quite so far as to say I feel completely disfigured, like I belong in a medical textbook or something, but... it definitely feels abnormal to me. It really does. 

And honestly, to give you a little context, this whole thing really started—or at least became this huge issue for me—because of a minor home improvement project, if you can believe that. We decided to update our master bathroom a little while ago, and we put in this new vanity setup with that really bright, modern LED lighting. You know the kind I mean? It's supposed to mimic natural daylight so it's better for applying makeup, but honestly, it is just so incredibly harsh. And I’m really here because ever since we put in that brighter bathroom mirror, I just keep noticing that the skin around my cheeks and jaw looks so incredibly uneven. It just looks kind of saggy to me, in a way that I had never, ever noticed before we changed out those fixtures. It’s like that new light catches every single little dip and droop and casts these awful shadows. 

And the most frustrating part about all of this—and the thing that really makes me feel like I’m losing my mind sometimes—is that my husband says he can’t really see what I’m talking about. I will literally stand there in the bathroom with him, with the bright lights on, pointing right at the exact spot on my jawline where the skin is sagging, trying to show him the unevenness, and he just looks at me blankly. He tells me I look exactly the same as I always have and that he doesn't see it at all. He thinks I'm making a mountain out of a molehill. 

But to me, it's right there. It is so glaringly obvious. I look in that mirror and I just see this sagging, uneven mess. So, even if I don't feel entirely "defective" as a whole human being, that specific part of my face feels so wrong and so unattractive to me now. It just dominates how I see myself when I look in the mirror, and I just can't unsee it, no matter what my husband says.
Do you believe that other people notice this issue with your jawline as much as you do, or do you think it's something that only you can really see?

Well, gosh, I... I don't really know for sure. It's so hard to tell what goes on in other people's heads, isn't it? I mean, like I was just saying about my husband, he swears up and down that he doesn't see a thing. He'll look right at the exact spot I'm pointing to and tell me I look fine. But then, you know, husbands are supposed to say that kind of thing, so I never really know if he's just trying to keep the peace so we can get on with our evening, or if he genuinely is just blind to it. 

But as for other people... I honestly couldn't tell you. I've never had anyone actually come up to me and say, "Wow, your jawline is really looking saggy lately," or anything horrible like that. People are usually too polite anyway, especially in a professional environment like the law firm. You know, HR would have an absolute field day if people went around commenting on each other's faces. So nobody says anything. But when I'm sitting there in a meeting, taking notes on a case, and one of the partners glances over at me... my mind just immediately goes, "Oh God, they're looking at the shadows under my chin." 

But do they actually see it? Are they noticing the unevenness, or are they just looking at me because they're waiting for me to hand them a file? I just... I really don't know. I feel like it's glaringly obvious, like this neon sign on my face, especially under those awful fluorescent lights in our main conference room. But since nobody actually points it out, I just spend half my day agonizing over whether they're secretly judging my skin or if it really is just something that only looks this terrible to me. It’s just this constant, exhausting guessing game in my head.
Do you feel that your concern about your jawline is something that is irrational or excessive, even if you can't seem to stop thinking about it?

Irrational... I mean, gosh, I really don't know. It’s hard to say. Sometimes I sit there at my desk, looking at the piles of depositions I have to summarize for the senior partner, and I think to myself, "Why are you letting this jawline thing consume so much of your mental energy?" So in that sense, maybe part of me knows it's taking up a bit too much space in my brain. Like, I know I shouldn't be thinking about my face when I'm trying to cross-reference case files and meet a filing deadline. 

But then... how can it be completely irrational if I can physically see it? It's not like I'm making it up out of thin air. I go home, I turn on that bright new vanity light we installed, and the sagging is just staring right back at me. I'll spend twenty minutes just gently pulling the skin back with my fingertips, just trying to see what it would look like if it were just a little tighter, you know, like it used to be before all this started. 

My husband, bless his heart, he definitely thinks it's excessive. He tells me I'm obsessing. Just the other night we were watching TV—one of those legal dramas that always gets the courtroom procedure completely wrong, which usually drives me crazy anyway—and I was just sitting there on the couch, absentmindedly rubbing my jawline, feeling the unevenness. He actually paused the show, turned to me, and gave me this whole speech about how I need to stop fixating on it and how it's taking over my evenings. 

So, is it excessive? I guess maybe it is, considering how much it interrupts my mornings and makes me dodge photos at book club like we talked about. But is it irrational? I just can't bring myself to say it's completely irrational when the flaw is actually there, visibly on my face. It's just this constant, exhausting battle in my head. I go back and forth on it a dozen times a day, trying to convince myself to just let it go and be sensible, and then immediately getting pulled right back into the panic the second I catch my reflection in the microwave door or a dark window. I just don't know what to think about it anymore.
Have there been times when you feel absolutely certain that your jawline looks severely unattractive or deformed, even when others don’t seem to notice anything wrong?

Well, yes, absolutely. I know I keep coming back to this, but like I was saying earlier about that new bathroom mirror... that really is the epicenter of all this for me. There are moments, especially right when I'm getting ready for work at the firm in the mornings, where I stand in front of that vanity and I am just... I am one hundred percent certain that it looks terrible. It's not just a passing thought, it's this heavy, sinking feeling of absolute certainty. 

I'll lean in close and look at the skin right around my cheeks and my jaw, and it just looks so distinctly uneven and saggy to me. It's like I can see gravity pulling it down in real-time, casting these deep, awful shadows. And then, just like I mentioned before, my husband will walk in to grab his toothbrush or his shaving cream, and I'll point right to the spot and ask him, "Don't you see how bad this side looks today? Doesn't it look worse than yesterday?" 

And he just... he doesn't get it. He'll squint and tilt his head and swear up and down that he can’t really see what I’m talking about at all. He'll say, "Honey, your face looks exactly the same as it did when we got married," which is sweet, I suppose, but it doesn't help me. It just makes me feel so isolated, you know? Because I am standing there, staring right at it, absolutely certain that it looks deformed and saggy, and it just blows my mind that he can stand two feet away and claim it looks completely fine. I'll even try to adjust the dimmer on those bright lights, thinking maybe if I just get the angle right, he'll finally see the unevenness that I'm seeing. But he never does. So, yes, I get very certain about it, and it's incredibly frustrating when it feels like I'm the only one living in this reality where my jawline is falling apart.
Has your concern about your jawline ever made you feel so anxious or self-conscious that you’ve had trouble interacting with others or felt unable to perform at work, even for a short time?

Oh, gosh, well... it hasn't completely stopped me from doing my job, if that's what you mean. I mean, I still get my work done. I have to. The firm doesn't stop just because I'm having a bad face day, you know? But, well, it definitely gets in the way of things. It really does. Like I was saying about those mornings in front of the mirror... the extra time I spend just staring and pulling at my skin, trying to get my makeup to sit exactly right so it hides the shadows... it adds up. It really adds up. 

There have definitely been a few mornings where I've lost track of time completely because I'm so focused on trying to fix it, and then suddenly I'm looking at the clock and I'm practically sprinting to my car. I've had to rush into the courthouse a few times, completely out of breath, just barely making it before the judge calls the docket, all because I couldn't tear myself away from the vanity. And it's not just work, either. I've missed the start of my Saturday morning yoga class more than once. I just get stuck in the bathroom, agonizing over whether I should even go if my face is going to look like that under the studio lights, and by the time I finally convince myself to just leave the house, the warm-up is already over. 

And then there's the social stuff. I think I mentioned my book club earlier? Well, I still go, mostly, but... it's the photos. You know how people are these days, always wanting to document every little get-together and post it on Facebook or whatever. Whenever someone pulls out their phone to take a group picture, I just... I panic a little bit. I've actually skipped out on a few casual photos at the book club, and even at a couple of community events we've gone to. I'll just suddenly remember I need to use the restroom, or I'll pretend I need to check my phone for an important email from the partners, just so I can step out of the frame. I just don't want to have to worry about how my jawline is going to look in the picture, forever immortalized on someone's timeline where I can't control the lighting or the angle. So, no, I haven't completely shut down or stopped working, but... it's definitely making things harder than they need to be. It just takes up so much time and energy.

Has there ever been a time when your concern about your jawline made you feel so distressed that you had trouble functioning normally—even for a short period—like difficulty concentrating, feeling anxious, or avoiding situations altogether?

Well, gosh, I feel like we're sort of circling back to exactly what I was just rambling on about, but yes, absolutely. I mean, like I was just saying, it hasn't completely derailed my entire life—I still get my work done, I haven't lost my job or anything drastic like that. I've always prided myself on being a reliable employee for the partners. But the distress... oh, the distress is definitely there, and it definitely throws a wrench into my normal routine. 

Just like I mentioned a second ago about those mornings when I get stuck in front of the bathroom vanity... the anxiety just builds and builds the longer I stand there looking at the sagging. And then I end up rushing into the courthouse, completely frantic. Do you have any idea how stressful it is to be practically sprinting up those heavy stone courthouse steps in heels, trying to shove my bag through the security scanner, knowing the judge is literally about to call the docket? And it's all because I couldn't stop obsessing over the shadows on my jawline for an extra twenty minutes. My heart will just be pounding out of my chest, and it's incredibly distressing to start my workday like that. 

And the avoidance... yes, exactly like I was just telling you about the photos. I avoid them like the plague now. I’ve skipped out on those casual photos at my book club, and my husband and I went to this community event recently—a sort of neighborhood block party thing—and I did the exact same routine there. The second someone pulled out their smartphone and yelled for everyone to squeeze in, I just felt this huge spike of pure anxiety in my chest, just absolute dread. I literally walked away and pretended to be intensely interested in a folding table full of raffle prizes just so I wouldn't have to worry about how my face would look in the picture. 

And then there's the yoga class I was telling you about... missing the start of it more than once because I'm just sitting at home, practically paralyzed by how my jaw looks in the mirror. Walking into the studio late while everyone is already on their mats, breathing and centering themselves, and the instructor gives you that look... it's humiliating. It just ruins the whole point of going to a relaxing class in the first place. So, yes, even though I'm still functioning on paper and getting my legal briefs filed, it really does cause a lot of internal panic and makes me avoid these little everyday things that I used to just do without a second thought. It's just exhausting.

Has your concern about your jawline ever caused you to feel so distressed that it interfered with your ability to engage in social activities, perform at work, or function normally in other important areas of your life, even temporarily?

I'm sorry, Doctor, I feel like I must be sounding like a broken record today, or maybe I'm just not explaining myself very well, because I feel like you're asking me the exact same thing again. But, well, yes... yes, it absolutely interferes, exactly in the ways I was just describing to you. 

I mean, to be perfectly clear, I still get my work done. I've been a paralegal for a long time, and the attorneys at the firm really rely on me, so I don't just completely fall apart or call in sick over this. I push through. But... it's the time. The sheer amount of time I spend getting ready in the mornings because I'm just paralyzed in front of that bathroom mirror, trying to do something, anything, about the sagging. That extra time has literally caused me to rush into the courthouse on a few mornings, completely flustered, out of breath, just praying I make it before the proceedings start. 

And it spills over into my personal time, too, just like I was saying. I've missed the start of my yoga class more than once. I'll just be sitting there at home, completely stuck, worrying about how my jaw is going to look under the studio lighting... and then you finally force yourself to go, and you walk in late and disrupt everybody's zen, which is just a terrible feeling. 

And socially... well, I'm still going to my book club and going to community events with my husband, but I've definitely skipped a few casual photos at those things. I'll just make up an excuse to walk away or check my phone because I simply cannot bear the thought of standing there, trying to smile naturally, while the whole time I'm just obsessing over how my face is going to look in the picture. I just don't want to worry about it, so I avoid the camera entirely. So, yes, even though I'm holding down my job and keeping up appearances, it absolutely causes distress and gets in the way of me just living my life normally.

Has your concern about your jawline ever caused you to feel so distressed that you had trouble functioning normally in important areas of your life, such as at work, in social situations, or in your personal well-being?

Doctor, I... I honestly don't know what else to tell you. Are you... did you not hear me the last three times? I feel like I'm just repeating the exact same words over and over again, and I really don't mean to be rude, I just... I don't understand why we keep circling back to this exact same question. I feel like I'm going a little crazy here! 

Let me try to just lay it out one more time, as plainly as I can, because maybe I'm just getting too caught up in my own stories and not giving you what you need. Yes, it causes distress. But no, I haven't stopped functioning. I still get my work done. I'm a dedicated employee, and the attorneys need me, so I make sure my work is handled. But the extra time I spend getting ready in the morning—just standing there, agonizing over my jawline and trying to hide the sagging—has made me rush into the courthouse a few mornings, completely panicked. And it's the same in my personal life. I've missed the start of my yoga class more than once because I get stuck at home obsessing over the mirror. 

And socially, like I literally just mentioned a minute ago, I’ve skipped a few casual photos at my book club and at those community events with my husband. I just walk away or make an excuse because I simply don’t want to worry about how my face is going to look in the pictures. It's just easier to avoid the camera altogether. So yes, it interferes, but I'm still living my life. I feel like I'm giving you all the details about how it affects my work and my social life, but maybe I'm missing whatever it is you're actually trying to ask me? Is there some specific detail I'm leaving out that you need to know?
Has your concern about your jawline ever caused you to feel so distressed that you considered seeking cosmetic procedures or medical interventions to fix it?

Oh, okay, a new question. Thank goodness, I was really starting to think we were stuck in some kind of weird loop there for a minute! 

But to answer this one... no. No, I haven't actually considered any real medical procedures or cosmetic surgery or anything drastic like that. I mean, don't get me wrong, obviously the sagging bothers me immensely—I think we've certainly covered that today!—but the thought of actually going to a plastic surgeon or getting things injected into my face? That just scares me half to death. 

You see these women, even some of the older female attorneys at the firm or the clients who come in for the high-asset divorces, and sometimes they just look so... I don't know, pulled tight? Like they're caught in a wind tunnel or they can't even show emotion anymore. I would be absolutely terrified of having a botched job or coming out looking completely unnatural, or having some horrible allergic reaction to whatever they pump into you. Plus, the cost! I'm a paralegal, I'm certainly not making partner money, so I couldn't even begin to justify spending thousands of dollars on something like that. 

So, no, no medical interventions. I just stick to spending way too much money on those expensive firming neck creams at the department store—you know, the ones in the heavy little glass jars that the sales ladies promise will work miracles but probably just sit on top of your skin and make you break out—and I just spend all that extra time in the morning trying to use contouring makeup to create a shadow where my jawline used to be. But as for actual procedures, no, I haven't crossed that bridge, and I really don't think I ever would. It just feels too extreme, even with how much the whole thing stresses me out.
Have there been times when you’ve had intrusive, unwanted thoughts about your jawline that you couldn’t stop thinking about, even when you tried not to focus on it?

Oh, intrusive is definitely the right word for it. I mean, it's funny you ask it that way, because I know exactly when this whole thing really took hold of me. 

We decided to do a little updating in our master bathroom a while back—nothing major, just some new fixtures and, crucially, a new vanity mirror. We put in one of those really modern ones, you know, with the built-in LED lights all the way around the edge that are supposed to mimic natural daylight and be so great for doing your makeup? Well, ever since we put in that brighter bathroom mirror, it’s like my eyes are just drawn straight to my lower face the second I walk into the room. I just keep noticing that the skin right around my cheeks and my jawline looks... well, uneven. Or just kind of saggy to me. 

And once I noticed it under that harsh lighting, I just couldn't unsee it. That's where the intrusive part really comes in. I'll be sitting at my desk at the firm, trying to focus on proofreading a fifty-page deposition, and suddenly I'm just completely distracted, obsessing over whether the sagging is noticeable to the attorneys under the office fluorescent lights. I try so hard to push the thought away and just focus on the paperwork, but it just keeps popping right back into my head. It’s like a tab left open in my brain that I can't close. 

And honestly, the most frustrating part of the whole thing—and I’ve brought this up to my husband so many times, probably more than he'd like—is that he says he can’t really see what I’m talking about! He looks right at me, right where I'm pointing, and swears he doesn't see the unevenness or the sagging at all. Which, you know, bless him, he's a good man and he's trying to be supportive, but it almost makes me feel crazier because *I* see it so clearly. It's right there. And because I know it's there, I just can't stop thinking about it, no matter how much I try to tell myself to let it go.

Do you feel intense anxiety or fear specifically in situations where you think others might closely notice or judge the appearance of your jawline, such as during face-to-face conversations or when being photographed?

Well, intense anxiety might be... I mean, I don't know if I'd use the word 'intense' like I'm having a full-blown panic attack or anything, but it definitely makes me incredibly self-conscious. Especially when I'm right up close to someone. If one of the partners comes over to my desk to review a brief with me, I catch myself sort of tilting my chin up or angling my head away so they don't get a direct profile view of the sagging. I just constantly worry they're looking right at it instead of listening to what I'm saying about the case.

And because of that worry... well, it's exactly why I have that whole morning routine I was telling you about. Most mornings, before I even step foot out the door, I end up standing in front of that bright bathroom mirror, checking my face from a few different angles. I'll turn to the left, then the right, tip my head down, just trying to see exactly how bad the unevenness looks that day from every possible perspective. And then I almost always end up putting on a little extra makeup, just trying to contour and blend it all in right before I leave for the courthouse. I just can't leave the house until I feel like I've hidden it as best as I possibly can. 

And then when I actually get to the firm... oh, it's terrible, but I just can't stop myself from comparing. I'll be in the breakroom pouring coffee or just walking down the hall, and I sometimes just find myself comparing my face to the other women I see at work.
